newsitem.title: USA: Large sized patterns from TV's "Designing Woman".
newsitem.headline: Large sized patterns from TV's "Designing Woman".

text.p: One in three, or about 47 million American women, wear a dress size 14 or larger. But if you look at fashion magazines, you would think it was one in three billion.
But reality is finally sinking in, with more designers and companies offering fashions for women who wear larger than a size 14. The options are also beginning to spill into fashions for home sewers.
Butterick Co., one of the nation's largest pattern companies, is introducing a new line of plus-size patterns in collaboration with actress Delta Burke, former star of television's "Designing Women."
"I came up with the idea for the line in general because of my own history with the weight," she said from a New York hotel, on a promotional tour here.

"I went through so much when I was putting on the weight," she said. "It was so very public" because of her celebrity status. Tabloids gave often exhaustive coverage to just about every ounce she gained or lost.
"I knew how I got so very depressed and down... I couldn't find anything in the stores, or (larger sizes) were stuck down in the basement like a freak."
Burke said she wants to give women "a more positive experience -- provide with more options in terms of sizes and other choices.
"It's all about how you feel emotionally. Also if you're given a tent to wear, there's no way to feel good."
Describing herself as "big and curvy" and feeling good about it, Burke said the patterns allow other women to think of themselves that way as well.
She said she thinks it is important for the patterns to have many style options, since many plus-size women like to emphasise specific features and de-emphasise others.
For example, she said she feels uncomfortable with bare arms, but "a lot of larger ladies don't." The patterns give sleeve options, among others.
Butterick said Burke is the first celebrity to collaborate with the company in over 15 years.

The Delta Burke collection, to be in sewing stores nationwide, consists of two dress styles and two sportswear styles, and each pattern has four variations. All are sized 14W to 30W with adjustment lines for petite sizes.
Each package sells for about $11.95.

BET Holdings Inc., owner of the cable station Black Entertainment Televsion, and G-III Apparel Group Inc. will produce a BET-branded clothing and accessory line catering to the African-American and urban consumer.
The line of outerwear, sportswear and accessories should be in select stores by the end of 1997, with national distribution expected next year.

G-III Apparel designs and distributes apparel under "G-III", "Siena" and "Siena Studio" labels. It also has a licensing agreement with Kenneth Cole Productions, National Football League Properties and the National Hockey League.

A BET spokeswoman said from company headquarters in Washington, D.C., the line is still in the planning stages but it is expected to include items for men and women such as pants, shirts and jackets. It also might include some higher end items as well, such as leather jackets, she said.
The clothing line, which represents BET's first foray into the fashion arena, will be sold in department stores and possibly mass marketers, depending on item and price, she said.
With bathing suit weather just around the corner in many parts of the country, many women dread the experience of shopping for one.
Swim Shaper, a New York-based swimsuit manufacturer, has developed Miraclesuit, a bathing suit that claims to make the wearer look 10 pounds lighter -- in the 10 seconds it takes to put it on.
The one-piece style swim suits are made from Miratex, a high performance fabric that contains three times more Lycra brand spandex than ordinary swimsuit fabrics, the company said.
The bathing suits come come in various bra sizes, missy sizes 6 to 18 and plus-sizes from 16W to 24W.
They sell from about $76 to $110.
For more information, call the company at 1-800-SWIM SHAPER (1-800-794-6742).
Here's help for those mortified by the reflection in a dressing room's three-sided mirror.
Bathing suit maker Jantzen Inc., which claims that four out of five bathing suit shoppers leave a store without making a swim suit purchase, has established the SwimFit Web site.
The Web site (www.jantzenswim.com), online as of Feb. 25, is an interactive personal fit-finder, designed to take into account a person's size and shape and help find a flattering suit.
